issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For an adult male sexual assault survivor, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the selected items and formulation. The other triggers (related news, motorcycle noise) plausibly cue intrusive memory reactivation, and the memory items are all intrusion/emotion based. 'Being around children' implies a distinct trauma meaning or developmental context that is not reflected anywhere in Memory, Threat, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies. Given the formulation is dominated by Triggers ↔ Memory links, this trigger stands out as insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory content and is the one item most likely to be incoherent.

vignette: The August night Tevita was thirty-two had ended in a dimly lit storage lot behind a downtown warehouse, where three men cornered him after a late shift. One of them had been drinking heavily, the sharp, yeasty tang of cheap liquor clinging to his coat as he spoke. The low, mechanical idle of a parked motorcycle echoed off the brick walls, a sound that vibrated through the asphalt until Tevita’s own chest tightened against the violence that followed. The assault was brief but devastating, leaving Tevita with a shattered sense of safety that lingered long after he limped home. In the months that followed, what frightened him most was not just the memory of the violence itself, but how quickly the world began to mirror it. A late-night news broadcast detailing a similar downtown attack made his pulse spike, and the smell of whiskey from a neighbor’s open window triggered a physiological freeze that left him unable to move. Tevita had come to believe that the past was bleeding into his present. When he recalled the night in the storage lot, his memories of the event felt more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, textured and immediate in a way that daytime routines never were. Sometimes, without a single clear picture, he would feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, a wave of panic and shame that arrived unannounced and left him hollow. Grief on recall would follow swiftly, a heavy, suffocating sorrow that made him stare at his kitchen table for hours, completely disconnected from his wife. What frightened him most was how the triggers themselves seemed to pull these memories forward; a passing motorcycle noise on the way to a job site would instantly summon the scent of alcohol to his mind, which then pulled the emotional memory back into the driver’s seat, making the past feel inescapable. To survive the mounting dread, Tevita began structuring his days around rigid control. He avoided physical stress by refusing to climb ladders or handle heavy shingles, opting instead for ground-level inspections that left his foreman bewildered. He restricted eating, counting every calorie and portion to feel in control when nothing else seemed manageable, and he worked hard at keeping busy with other things, layering calls, estimates, and weekend projects over his evenings. These strategies initially quieted the panic, but they also carved out a fragile routine that kept him perpetually on edge. When a news report surfaced about a nearby assault, the sudden spike in anxiety made it impossible to concentrate, and he would immediately retreat to his safe, predictable patterns of avoidance and dietary restriction, using busyness to outrun the dread. Over time, the habits he relied on to stay grounded began to fracture under their own weight. Restricting eating and avoiding physical stress left his body in a state of chronic hypervigilance, lowering his threshold for every environmental cue. The busyness he depended on to keep moving only delayed the inevitable; when he finally sat alone after a long day on the roof, the distraction vanished, and emotion without image would rush in to fill the silence. His mind clung to the grief on recall, which in turn sharpened his attention to every motorcycle noise, every news alert, and every whiff of alcohol, making the triggers feel more potent than ever. The more he tried to suppress the past through strict routines and relentless activity, the more his nervous system braced for the next assault, turning his daily survival tactics into the very engine of his distress. The tightening cycle eventually reached his marriage and his work. His wife noticed how he flinched when the garbage truck’s engine backfired, mirroring those motorcycle sounds, and how he withdrew during family dinners to maintain his strict eating schedule. At forty-eight, Tevita found himself exhausted by the constant surveillance of his own body, his PCL-5 score of 47 a quiet testament to the toll. He finally sat across from a therapist, not because he wanted to relive the storage lot night, but because he was terrified that if he stopped moving or stopped counting, the grief on recall would swallow him whole. He hoped, desperately, to find a way to stand on a roof again without bracing for impact, and to finally let the past stay exactly where it belonged.
